title: CVE-2026-135279 - @fastify/express vulnerable to middleware bypass via empty route parameters in Express routers and sub-applications
text:
9.1

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-135279
@fastify/express vulnerable to middleware bypass via empty route parameters in Express routers and sub-applications

@fastify/express is the plugin that lets an application run Express middleware and Express applications inside the Fastify web framework. In versions before 4.0.14, a request with an empty dynamic route parameter reaches a Fastify route handler while middleware mounted for that path inside an Express Router or sub-application is skipped, because Fastify's router accepts an empty value where Express requires a non-empty one, and an unanchored regular-expression mount passed to the plugin is bypassed the same way. An earlier fix covered only the mount paths passed to the plugin directly, not middleware mounted inside a routed Express application. An attacker can use this to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on the affected routes, with the practical impact depending on what the empty value selects in the application. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.14, and users should upgrade to 4.0.14 or later. As a workaround, enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, mount the middleware on a static parent path, or require non-empty values in the route params schema.

Victims download a working wallpaper app that also installs malicious components in the background.No activity observed from Vietnam: Bitdefender telemetry did not record SYS010-related activity from Vietnam. This is consistent with, but does not prove, the possibility that Vietnamese-speaking individuals may be operating the campaign while targeting people elsewhere.From PHP Infostealer to PHP loader: The PHP samples no longer steal data. They enroll the victim with the command and control (C2) server and wait for tasks, and the next stages are delivered only to the victims that the server selects.The Infostealer moved into the browser: The final payload is a malicious browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox that can steal browser cookies and collect data from Facebook ad accounts, Business Managers and Pages. title: What is Strategic Threat Intelligence? | Recorded Future
text:
PUBLISHED ON 26 NOV 2026

Recorded Future

Key Takeaways
Threat intelligence is often thought of as a single function, but in reality, it can be broken down into four categories: strategic, tactical, operational, and technical.
Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical and is used by high-level strategists to inform specific decisions.
For the most part, strategic threat intelligence comes from freely available sources. However, the volume of available sources, combined with language constraints, often makes manual collection infeasible.
The success of strategic threat intelligence depends on strong two-way communication between threat analysts and their primary audience — usually the board of directors.
On the surface, threat intelligence appears to be a single discipline, closely intertwined with the cyber threat intelligence cycle. Practitioners collect data from a variety of sources, analyze it, and use the outputs to make decisions.The reality is a little more complicated. As with most specialties, threat intelligence can be broken down into subcategories, each with its own uses, techniques, and challenges. Here are the three distinct categories that threat intelligence is typically boiled down to:
Strategic Intelligence: Non-technical, risk-based intelligence used by high-level decision makers.
Tactical Intelligence: Details of threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
Operational Intelligence: Actionable information about specific incoming attacks.
In this blog series, we’ll take an in-depth look at each of these categories, including how they are collected, analyzed, and used to enhance security.Today, we’re covering strategic intelligence.What Is Strategic Threat Intelligence?Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical, risk-focused intelligence that provides executives and board members with a bird’s-eye view of an organization’s threat landscape, enabling them to understand the broader impact of high-level business decisions. It isn’t concerned with specific actors, indicators, or attacks.Given that the audience is primarily C-suite and board level, strategic threat intelligence is almost exclusively non-technical. Instead, it covers factors such as risk scores and the possible outcomes of a given action or decision, such as entering a foreign market or taking an ideological position.Since it’s used to inform specific, high-level decisions, strategic threat intelligence is usually gathered on demand rather than as an ongoing initiative, and is most often presented as a report or briefing.Sources of Strategic Threat IntelligenceUnlike other intelligence categories, the majority of strategic threat intelligence sources are Open Source Intelligence, or OSINT, meaning they can be freely accessed by anyone who cares to do so. Policy documents from nation-states and other groups of interest
Local and national media
Industry- and subject-specific publications
Comments, online activity, and articles from individuals of interest
Free content produced by security organizations (e.g., white papers, research reports, etc.)

title: How a Fake Job Interview Led to the $6.34 Billion Binance Theft
text: Jump to sectionIn September 2026, a software engineer at Binance got a message on a job-hunting site. Someone posing as a Project Director wanted to talk about a role. What followed looked like a normal hiring process. First came a live video interview with an HR representative, then a second round with someone claiming to be the CEO. Near the end of that call, the engineer was told to download a coding assignment. He did it on his work computer, and malicious code gave the attackers access to his machine and credentials.The attackers moved laterally through the Binance organization, and on October 29 they stole about $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency. Binance's report lists the fake interview as one step in a longer chain. The developer wasn't the end goal. A candidate who runs an assignment on a work laptop hands the attackers a machine inside their employer's network.The FBI attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, the same North Korean group it blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025. Blockchain analysts at TRM Labs and Chainalysis also linked the two thefts, saying the attack matched Bybit in a few ways:The attackers started preparing at least 36 hours ahead.The signatures were produced in advance as a batch, then used in one burst.Three small Tornado Cash withdrawals funded the attackers' operator wallet.None of these alone proves it's the same group. They're patterns TRM has seen in earlier North Korean heists, and TRM paired them with on-chain and off-chain intelligence it didn't detail. Chainalysis said its strongest evidence was watching Binance funds mix in real time with proceeds from the roughly $357 million theft from crypto exchange Bitget in late September. Elliptic had already tied that hack to TraderTraitor in a preliminary assessment, citing on-chain overlaps with the Bybit attack. That chain of overlaps, from Binance to Bitget to Bybit, is the clearest public link between the attacks.The fake interview that compromised Binance follows the same playbook as Contagious Interview, a North Korean campaign that's been luring developers with fake job offers since at least 2023. That matters for defenders, but not as much as you might hope. Being able to detect Contagious Interview (or PolinRider, more on that below) activity is a good start. But it won't reliably catch TraderTraitor, which tailors its attacks to a small number of high-value targets. And no tool on the market today will stop a developer from consuming a malicious repository in the first place.TraderTraitor vs. Contagious Interview vs. PolinRiderThese names are easy to mix up, and they can overlap in practice. title: #NFS2ROOT: a 12-year-old pre-auth remote root in the Linux kernel's NFS server https://opensec.in/blog/nfs2root-cve-2026-99362 #infosec #sysadmin
text:
Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in. We pointed OpenSec's Antara at it. It came back with a root shell.
CVSS9.8criticalAdvisoryCVE-2026-99362criticalCVSS 9.8Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd)
Fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1. Update the kernel and reboot.

What you need to know
What: a pre-auth heap overflow in the kernel's NFS server, nfsd.
Who: any Linux host serving NFSv4.1 or 4.2 (the default) on a reachable tcp/2049.
Impact: one TCP connection writes 61 bytes past a kernel heap object; chained, that gives a root shell.
Now: patch and reboot. Until then, firewall tcp/2049.

Key facts
Severity 9.8 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N)
Attack Remote, unauthenticated, tcp/2049
Impact Kernel heap overflow → remote root shell
Bug age 12 years, since Linux 3.16 (2014)
Affected In-kernel nfsd with NFSv4.1 or 4.2
Fixed in 6.12.117 · 6.18.61 · 7.3.2 · 7.4-rc1

One connection, no login#
The NFS server runs inside the kernel and parses network input before it knows who you are. CVE-2026-99362 lives in that gap: a client can shrink its reply cache to zero bytes, then make the server copy a full reply into it. The copy lands on the kernel heap, and the client picks most of the bytes.
How NFS2ROOT reaches a Linux NFS server: one unauthenticated TCP connection to port 2049
Twelve years in a few lines of C#
TimelineMar 2014Commit 47ee52986472 narrows the reply buffer while handling SEQUENCE. It ships in Linux 3.16.2014 to 202612 yearsEvery kernel since 3.16 carries it: LTS, distribution and appliance kernels.17 Aug 2026Jérémy Jean of ANSSI sends a fix upstream with a KASAN report.21 Sep 2026OpenSec's Antara flags the bug, scores it 9.8 and turns it into a root shell on its own.20 Nov 2026CVE-2026-99362 is published with fixes.
Watch it run#
A real run, end to end. Left: the victim's console. Right: our client on another machine, talking to the victim only over tcp/2049.
VideoNFS2ROOT recording: an unauthenticated client gets a root shell on a Linux NFS server
The overflow. The kernel warns in nfsd4_check_resp_size, but the out-of-bounds copy has already happened.
Root. The attacker hangs up, and the victim's kernel runs our command: root, then uid=0(root), then power-off.
Root cause#
Each NFSv4.1 session slot caches its last reply, so a retried request is answered exactly once. The client decides how big that cache is.
Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing.
KASAN report from the upstream fixtextCopyBUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390
Write of size 80 at addr ffff888003a549cd
__asan_memcpy+0x38/0x60
read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390
nfsd4_sequence_done+0x5b0/0x810
nfs4svc_encode_compoundres+0x1bf/0x240
That is 80 bytes copied, 61 of them past the end of the heap object, 40 of them chosen by the client.
Inside NFS2ROOT: the reply is copied into a slot buffer with no room for it.
The fix checks that the reply fits before taking the slot, and makes the encoder report what it can't fit.
From overflow to root#
The exploit stays private. Each step is an ordinary NFS request:
OverflowThe write corrupts the neighbouring slot's bookkeeping.LeakA replay request returns 3.8 KB of kernel heap, and with it the KASLR slide.FreeA forged pointer makes the kernel free an object we choose.ReclaimWe refill that memory with a fake callback built from NFS client names.TriggerWe hang up. nfsd calls the fake callback, and the kernel runs /bin/sh as root.

text:
Key takeaways

Through the attack on PLAID's KARTE platform, Japan's largest fashion shopping site and two of its three megabanks have reported leaks in the tens of millions: ZOZO about 15.18 million ZOZOTOWN customers and 13.93 million WEAR users, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) up to about 14 million records, and MUFG Bank about 6.5 million.
All three say the data cannot identify anyone: no names, addresses or account numbers, only things like birth dates, ages, genders, postcodes or regions, internal member IDs and flags.
That is true for an attacker holding these records alone. It is not true for the companies, which can link each record back to a customer. MUFG and ZOZO say they will contact the people concerned individually, which only works because they can. Japan's privacy law counts data that can be readily matched to a person as personal information.
In our view, the useful question is not whether a record has a name in it, but why a marketing tool needed it at all. SMBC sent both a full birth date and an age band. ZOZO's data included people who had left. Send a marketing tool the coarsest data that does the job, under an ID that means nothing elsewhere, and delete it when it is no longer needed.

title: 🚨🔓 SIGINT // Cybersecurity Watch — 2026-11-27 US Treasury's FinCEN proactively disconnected systems after unauthorized access, marking the latest breach in a wave targeting federal agencies. https://www.securityweek.com/us-treasurys-fincen-disconnects-systems-following-cyber-incident/ #Cybersecurity #InfoSec #DataBreach #FinCEN
text:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the US Treasury Department’s financial intelligence unit, has disconnected some of its systems while investigating a cyber incident.

“FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline,” the agency said in a notice on the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing System website.

The website is operational, but some FinCEN services may be temporarily unavailable, and the agency has extended the deadlines for qualifying filers affected by the disruption.

“FinCEN is granting temporary, limited exceptive relief in response to a service disruption that is hindering filers’ ability to adhere to reporting obligations,” the agency said in a November 24 order (PDF).

The agency has not shared further details on the nature of the incident and made no mention of a potential data breach, but said it was working to return all systems to normal.

It is unclear who was behind the attack and if any data was accessed or stolen. SecurityWeek has emailed FinCEN for additional information and will update this article if the agency responds.

FinCEN disclosed the incident amid a wave of cyberattacks and outages impacting US government agencies, including the CIA, which had an unclassified system breached.

FIFA Hack: 12 GB Claimed, Under 0.1% of Data Hit

Dr. Elena Marchetti
Updated Nov 26, 2026 · 16 min read

Photo: MCaviglia digimen.ch, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons FIFA said on November 26, 2026 that it was the victim of a criminal cyberattack, and AP News carried the statement that attackers gained unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information. That sentence is the confirmed core of the FIFA cyberattack story. Almost everything around it, from the size of the haul to the identity of the culprits, still rests on claims that FIFA has not verified.

The governing body of world football runs the World Cup, licenses broadcast rights worldwide and sits on years of agreements with governments, sponsors and member associations. A breach at an organization like that matters even when the headline wording is cautious. As with the Zodia Custody breach we covered today, the first disclosure arrived with data types named and counts left out.

This analysis separates what FIFA and Reuters have put on the record from what attackers and analysts allege. It also looks at what the incident could mean for people and organizations that deal with FIFA, how the disclosure compares with other recent breaches, and which questions will decide how serious this turns out to be. Every claim below is attributed to a named outlet, and anything unverified is labelled that way.

·Google · Preferred SourcesDon't miss new tech stories on GoogleAdd Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.Add nowWhat FIFA Confirmed About the Cyberattack

FIFA’s own statement is short. The organization said it was the victim of a criminal cyberattack that resulted in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information. It said it is working with relevant authorities, including law enforcement. And it condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data.

Three details stand out in that wording. First, FIFA called the incident criminal, which signals an outside party and not an accidental exposure or a misconfigured server. Second, the phrase “limited set” frames the scope without quantifying it. Third, the condemnation of “acquisition and publication” suggests that some of the material has already been released or threatened with release, although FIFA did not say what has been published or where.

The Athletic, part of The New York Times, ran the story under a headline saying FIFA was the subject of a cyberattack and had personal and business information stolen. TechRadar framed it as a hack in which threat actors accessed the same two categories. NBC News and The Times also covered the announcement the same day. The wording across outlets matches FIFA’s, which tells us the organization issued a single controlled statement and did not take follow-up questions in detail.

What FIFA did not say

FIFA did not state when the attack occurred. It did not say how many people or organizations were affected. It did not describe what the business information contained. Those three gaps define the story today, and reporting from several outlets points to the same omissions.

The attack method is also unconfirmed. No outlet in the coverage reviewed for this piece has verified whether the intrusion came through stolen credentials, a third-party vendor, a software flaw or something else. Without that, defenders at other organizations cannot yet extract a technical lesson.

The 12 GB Claim and What Remains Unverified

The most quoted number in this story comes from the attackers’ side, not from FIFA. TechRadar reported that hackers claim 12.2 GB of data was stolen, while Soapcentral’s headline put the figure at 12GB. FIFA has not confirmed either number, and independent verification is missing. Treat 12 GB as a claim and nothing more.

On November 20, 2026, Bell Canada, one of Canada's largest telecommunications companies, confirmed it is investigating a cybersecurity incident where a threat actor breached its systems and stole data. The company described the intruder as an "agentic threat actor," a term suggesting the use of AI-powered tools or autonomous techniques in the attack. The breach, which occurred on November 17, involved unauthorized access to a pre-production environment of its IBM Maximo system, which is used for managing telecom network connections. The attacker successfully exfiltrated data belonging to some of Bell's enterprise customers. Bell has since contained the incident and is working with law enforcement.

Threat Overview
The attack was first revealed through a breach notification sent to a Bell enterprise customer, which was then reported by BleepingComputer. Bell's subsequent investigation confirmed the intrusion. The threat actor, labeled "agentic," gained access to a non-production system. This is a common pattern where attackers target less-secure development or staging environments to find a foothold into an organization.
The compromised data includes:

Business contact information: Names, job titles, corporate email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.
Service-related information: Ticket titles from the Maximo system and some IP addresses associated with network systems.

Bell has asserted that the stolen dataset did not contain credentials, highly sensitive personal information, or file attachments. The company has not provided further details on the techniques used by the "agentic" actor or attributed the attack to any specific group.
Technical Analysis
The use of the term "agentic threat actor" is novel and suggests a level of automation beyond simple scripting. This could imply the use of AI-powered tools for reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, or lateral movement, similar to the Cairn framework seen in other recent attacks. However, without more detail from Bell, this remains speculative.
The known TTPs include:

Accessing Non-Production Environments: Attackers often target pre-production, staging, or development systems because they are typically less monitored and may have weaker security controls or default credentials. This relates to T1078 - Valid Accounts if default or weak credentials were used.
Data Exfiltration (T1041): The actor successfully exfiltrated a subset of enterprise customer data.
Data from Information Repositories (T1213): The attacker accessed and stole data from the Maximo application database.

Impact Assessment
The primary impact is on the affected Bell enterprise customers. The stolen contact and service information can be used by threat actors to launch highly convincing and targeted attacks, such as:

Spear-Phishing: Emails targeting specific employees with knowledge of their role and existing Bell services.
Vishing/SMiShing: Voice or SMS-based phishing attacks using the stolen phone numbers.
Business Email Compromise (BEC): Impersonating Bell employees or the enterprise customer's own staff to commit fraud.

The breach also carries reputational damage for Bell Canada and highlights the critical importance of securing non-production environments with the same rigor as production systems.

The attack on the EU Academy platform marks a significant public acknowledgment of an AI-assisted attack against a major government institution. The incident underscores the dual-use nature of AI tools, which can be repurposed for malicious activities.

An unauthorized actor discovered this endpoint and used it to access sensitive information, including customer contact details and, critically, cloud storage credentials for a subset of its more than 12,500 customers. The exposed credentials included keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS) S3 and Microsoft Azure Blob Storage. Radware detected and stopped the access after approximately ten hours but has warned that the stolen keys are being actively used in attacks. The company is urging all potentially affected customers to rotate their credentials immediately.
Threat Overview
This incident is a stark reminder of the risks associated with misconfigured cloud infrastructure and insecure APIs. The failure to secure an internal, privileged API provided a direct path for attackers to compromise customer data and infrastructure.

What Happened: An unauthenticated internal management API was exposed to the public internet.
Attack Vector: Direct access to the exposed API endpoint.
Data Compromised: Customer contact information and, for some, credentials for cloud services (AWS S3, Azure Blob, SFTP) used for log exports.

Technical Analysis
The root cause of the breach was a critical security misconfiguration, a common problem in complex cloud environments. An API endpoint intended for internal use was deployed with a public IP address and no authentication mechanism. This is a failure in access control, violating the principle of least privilege and secure-by-default design.
The attack followed a simple path:

Discovery: The threat actor discovered the exposed API endpoint, likely through internet-wide scanning (T1595.002 - Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning).
Exploitation: The actor accessed the API to enumerate and exfiltrate data. This falls under T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application.

The Perimeter Desk
Threat Wrap

2026-11-26

# The fragility of privileged identities

The most surprising news on the wire today isn't a massive data dump or a sophisticated state-sponsored exploit. It's the fact that hackers breached the FBI's criminal database. This is the system used for warrants, traffic stops, and tracking violent or wanted persons.

When we talk about "critical infrastructure," we usually mean power grids or water treatment plants. But a law enforcement database of this nature is operational infrastructure. The immediate concern isn't just data privacy; it's officer safety. If an attacker can see who is being hunted or modify the status of a warrant, they aren't just stealing records—they're manipulating the physical reality of police work on the street. This is a second-order effect that usually gets lost in the noise of "records exposed." The officers relying on that data during a high-risk stop are now operating with a compromised source of truth.

The sheer volume of attacks on government entities remains staggering. Government is currently the top targeted sector, with 454 stories this week and 87 new incidents reported today alone. It's becoming clear that the public sector isn't just a target of opportunity; it's a target of strategic utility.

This brings us to a specific tradecraft trend appearing in the 1Password breach. For those who haven't tracked the details, customer data and source code were stolen not through a flaw in 1Password's hardened vault, but via the compromise of a single employee's GitHub account.

We need to stop pretending that the "corporate perimeter" exists. The actual perimeter is now the identity of the developer. In this case, the attacker didn't need to break the encryption or find a zero-day in the product; they just needed the credentials of someone who had legitimate access to the code and the keys. This is an exercise in efficiency. Why spend six months trying to crack a vault when you can spend six days phishing a developer?

This rhymes with the SolarWinds campaign from 2020, though the parallel breaks at the point of entry. SolarWinds was a systemic failure of the build pipeline—the "factory" was poisoned. The 1Password incident is different because it's a failure of identity management for a privileged human. One was a structural flaw; the other is a credential flaw.

My position is this: as long as we treat developer accounts as "employees" rather than "high-value assets," these breaches will continue. A lead engineer's GitHub account should be treated with the same security rigor as a root password for a production database, including mandatory hardware keys and restricted access windows. Anything less is negligence.

I have moderate confidence in this assessment. To move to high confidence, I would need to see evidence that these attackers are systematically targeting developers across multiple firms using a unified set of stolen session tokens rather than opportunistic phishing.

On the topic of attribution, there's a lot of noise regarding "AI-driven" attacks. Specifically, the report that 24 Check Point management servers were compromised in an AI-powered campaign, and Microsoft's claim that Salt Typhoon is using an AI tool called Artex to accelerate intrusions.

I distrust these labels. My confidence level here is low.

In my experience, "AI-driven" has become a convenient shorthand for "the attacker moved faster than our detection windows allowed." Until I see the actual binaries or evidence of autonomous decision-making in the C2 traffic, I assume this is just highly optimized scripting. To change my mind, I'd need to see an exploit chain that adapts its payload in real-time based on the target's EDR response without human intervention.

1Password Discloses Data Breach Following Employee GitHub Account Compromise

1Password, a Toronto-based password management provider, disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to its internal systems, on November 25, 2026. The company began investigating the incident on November 19 after discovering that an employee's corporate GitHub account had been compromised.The attacker used the compromised account to access private source code repositories and deploy malicious code to backend services, allowing them to download customer account information. The attacker also copied source code and accessed the company's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which contained internal credentials. The exposed information includes:Customer names and email addressesAccount and user identifiersAccount creation and last sign-in timestampsPublic keys and Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parametersTokens from invitation, provisioning, and account recovery emailsInternal account metadata and version identifiersThe number of affected individuals has not been disclosed. The breach affected a subset of 1Password customers. Customer vaults, stored passwords, encryption keys, and account recovery keys were not compromised. The company's applications and browser extensions remain unaffected.1Password disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked unauthorized access, and rotated potentially exposed internal credentials. The company restored clean versions of the affected services. A small number of users with active provisioning or recovery tokens were notified directly. The company found no internal evidence of customer account takeovers involving the exposed provisioning tokens.Customers should be cautious of phishing messages, unexpected account invitations, and recovery requests. 1Password does not require customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys. Users should never share these credentials in response to unexpected emails, calls, or messages.

L’affaire Nvidia renvoie à des visions fondamentalement opposées de la stratégie technologique, bien au-delà de l’espionnage présumé et des lignes de fracture politiques. Derrière le retour de Jensen Huang à la tête de l’entreprise s’est manifestée l’opposition entre les intérêts des fournisseurs de modèles d’intelligence artificielle (IA), comme Anthropic ou OpenAI, et ceux des acteurs de l’infrastructure physique, en particulier des entreprises de semi-conducteurs, comme Nvidia. Bien que ces acteurs soient liés par un réseau complexe d’investissements circulaires, le secteur des semi-conducteurs capte l’essentiel de la valeur de l’IA, portée par des investissements massifs dans les infrastructures de calcul, tandis que les fournisseurs de modèles, de leur côté, peinent à trouver leur modèle économique.

Cette divergence est accrue par le développement de systèmes reposant sur l’IA agentique, qui accroît fortement la demande de capacité de calcul, tandis que les modèles ouverts, chinois en particulier, mettent sous pression la tarification des modèles fermés. La tendance est généralement à l’industrialisation de l’usage de l’IA et au développement de solutions sur mesure, de plus en plus autonomes vis-à-vis des environnements propriétaires.

Pour les pays en situation de vassalité technologique, l’approche combinant l’usage agentique de modèles ouverts et le recours direct aux infrastructures de calcul offre justement la perspective d’une mobilisation de l’IA à des fins de souveraineté et de rattrapage, par automatisation, à condition de mettre à contribution les compétences réelles.

Deux visions concurrentes de l’avenir de l’IA

Le système de financements circulaires entre les entreprises du secteur les a unies, pendant un temps, face à la difficulté à pleinement facturer les services d’IA. Les investissements des entreprises de semi-conducteurs permettent typiquement aux fournisseurs de modèles d’IA de leur acheter des puces, avec ces sommes. Cette unité vole en éclat à l’heure de la redoutable concurrence des modèles chinois et de l’IA agentique, qui marque une phase désormais industrielle de l’utilisation de l’IA.

La concurrence des modèles chinois ouverts exerce une pression considérable sur les prix. Des modèles performants, accessibles à moindre coût et pouvant être déployés localement, réduisent la capacité des fournisseurs payants à développer leurs marges. La consommation explose avec l’essor des usages agentiques. Les agents IA enchaînent de longues séquences d’itérations variées pour accomplir des tâches complexes. Cette évolution engendre une demande massive de capacité de calcul, mais ne garantit pas des profits ni présents ni futurs aux fournisseurs d’IA fermées. Les volumes augmentent mais les prix facturés à l’usage diminuent fortement.

Alors que Nvidia cherche à vendre toujours davantage de capacités de calcul et à étendre le marché, les fournisseurs de modèles propriétaires fermés doivent maîtriser leurs coûts et trouver des modèles de rentabilité durables. La concurrence des modèles ouverts et le développement de solution agentique « maison » par les entreprises, les met en péril. Leurs efforts massifs consistant à annoncer les prouesses de leurs modèles, notamment par le biais de démonstrations mathématiques majeures, s’inscrivent aussi dans ce contexte très compétitif.

De plus, Anthropic et OpenAI sont tentées d’alerter sur les risques existentiels, afin de freiner la course dans le développement de modèles et réduire ainsi le rythme de leurs dépenses vertigineuses. En effet, des restrictions importantes sont susceptibles de relever les barrières à l’entrée et de protéger les acteurs déjà établis au détriment de nouveaux concurrents disposant de moyens plus limités. Le sommet de la Coopération économique pour l’Asie-Pacifique (APEC) s’est tenu à Shenzhen du 18 au 19 novembre 2026 afin de discuter autour d’enjeux liés aux énergies propres, aux chaînes d’approvisionnement, à l’intelligence artificielle et au libre-échange. La Chine accueille ce sommet pour la troisième fois, cette année, il se démarque notamment par une rencontre trilatérale inédite entre les États-Unis, la Chine et la Russie. Quel bilan peut-on dresser du sommet de l’APEC 2026 ? Quel est le message politique derrière la rencontre trilatérale des trois plus grandes puissances ? Par conséquent, dans quelle direction la rivalité sino-américaine évolue-t-elle ? Le point avec Emmanuel Lincot, directeur de recherche à l’IRIS et co-responsable du Programme Asie-Pacifique

Que peut-on retenir de ce sommet ?

La presse chinoise a fait état d’un « nouveau Yalta », ce qui n’est qu’une pure vision de l’esprit. Rappelons qu’historiquement, Yalta avait eu lieu afin d’organiser des élections dans les pays libérés à l’issue de la Seconde Guerre mondiale. En cela, Yalta aura été trahi quelques mois plus tard par le sommet de Potsdam ; lequel consacrera un partage effectif du monde. Rien de tout cela à Shenzhen même si les trois acteurs ont signé une « déclaration de paix » commune sur la stabilité stratégique, sans aborder directement l’Ukraine. Statu quo ou presque même si les trois puissances ont déclaré vouloir dialoguer sur la réduction des risques nucléaires et la non-prolifération. Xi Jinping a défendu la levée des barrières commerciales et la mondialisation comme contre-modèle face à la ligne « America First » de Donald Trump. Des gestes ciblés ont eu lieu, comme la suspension temporaire par Pékin des droits de douane sur 400 millions de dollars d’exportations canadiennes. En revanche, la trêve commerciale entre la Chine et les États-Unis, qui arrive à échéance en janvier 2027, n’a fait l’objet et pour l’heure d’aucune prorogation. Si Xi Jinping a réussi à attirer l’attention des médias internationaux et permis à Shenzhen – que l’on appelle parfois la « Silicon valley chinoise » – de bénéficier, à cette occasion, d’une réelle dynamique sur le plan économique, comme en avait bénéficié Shanghai en 2008 à l’occasion de l’exposition universelle, dans les faits, on ne voit aucune avancée significative dans sa rivalité contre Donald Trump. Par ailleurs, ce dernier avait rencontré quelques jours plus tôt les membres de l’Association des nations de l’Asie du Sud-Est (ASEAN) et échangé avec le Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD) sur fond de frictions entre la Chine et respectivement les Philippines et Taïwan, mais aussi dans un contexte de dégradation inquiétante de la relation entre Tokyo et Pékin. Cet objectif sera sans aucun doute poursuivi au sommet de l’APEC 2027 qui se tiendra au Viêtnam, sur l’île de Phu Quoc.

title: Views from Ukraine on Digitalised Warfare
text: A Ukrainian soldier handling a drone controller and satellite communications. Image: Владимир Щербак / Alamy StockUkraine’s digitalised warfare owes less to AI than to integrating systems and data under strong authority – lessons the UK and NATO should heed.The war in Ukraine has been dominated by headlines about the cutting edge of technology in warfare, especially in the automation of functions and processes by AI. Yet AI and automation are not proving as consequential to operational successes as those efforts to integrate capabilities into coherent digital architectures. To draw the right lessons from Ukraine’s digitalised warfare experiences, one must consider the constraints and frictions in its uses of AI and automation, especially in the context of its disunified IT capabilities. Similarly, the manner through which situational awareness platforms like DELTA are integrated should be considered for NATO, with specific lessons on flexibility in data integration layers and the role of a strong implementation authority for the UK’s Digital Targeting Web.This article draws on the author’s observations and conversations from Ukraine.The Limits of AI and AutomationWhile the digitalisation of the Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) is justifiably lauded, it would not be accurate to call the AFU a truly automated nor AI-enabled force. Platforms and C2 (command and control) systems frequently have tasks automated – sometimes using AI – but the automation of full functions and processes is not widespread.The deployment of AI, especially machine learning models, is entirely reliant upon large quantities of high-quality data to both train and operate models, thereby requiring integrated data feeds. Essentially, AI allows for efficient exploitation of outputs from systems that have already been integrated. Absent the fusion of data streams alongside networking and hosting infrastructure, these algorithms are useless. And despite the advances in integration through common C2, air defence, and situational awareness platforms (see more below), the relatively decentralised nature of the AFU and its innovation renders it often difficult to obtain reliable feeds of the necessary data for even routine situational awareness, much less the consistent, high-fidelity datasets necessary for advanced models to function accurately.quoteThe manner through which these technologies are developed, deployed, integrated and iterated is as much of import as the capabilities themselves This is why the current use cases for AI have been predominantly very narrow tasks. Ukrainian systems frequently use machine vision to identify and track objects in video feeds on edge devices, such as deployed sensors and strike and ISR drones, or use relatively-simple AI models to assist navigation in global-navigation-satellite-system-denied (or Starlink-denied) environments. Yet it is rare for platforms to perform more than these combat tasks, especially when it comes to combat engagement of enemy systems. For example, Ukraine's Sky Sentinel turrets are theoretically capable of autonomous engagement of enemy drones, but this capability is rarely, if ever, used. Korea Investment Savings Bank leaks data of 86,433 customers, largest breach in financial sector

Korea Investment Savings Bank has suffered a personal data breach affecting approximately 86,000 customers. It is the largest such incident involving a savings bank and ranks among the biggest data breaches in South Korea's financial sector.

The bank said Wednesday that it had confirmed the leak of some customers' personal information following unauthorized external transactions on its mobile website.

"We confirmed during a system inspection on Nov. 23 that some customers' personal information had been leaked due to abnormal external transactions targeting our mobile website between 10:42 p.m. on Nov. 22 and 3:35 a.m. on Nov. 23," the bank said.

Korea Investment Savings Bank said that immediately after recognizing the personal information leak, it blocked the relevant IP address and illegal access routes and suspended the operation of related services. It added that it has completed necessary emergency measures, including applying new security policies and system monitoring, and strengthened security.

It further added, "We are taking this matter very seriously and will strengthen our internal management system to prevent recurrence of similar incidents, while continuously making every effort to protect customers' personal information."

To prevent secondary damage using the leaked personal information, one must not respond to spam emails aimed at voice phishing calls and texts, or distributing malicious code. One should also avoid clicking links of unknown origin or complying with requests for personal information input.

If damages occur due to personal information, one can calculate the amount of damages and file a civil lawsuit (damages claim suit) against Korea Investment Savings Bank. Additionally, if a personal information leak is acknowledged, damages can be claimed through civil litigation procedures without proving actual damages.

Recently, savings banks have suffered consecutive data breach damages due to hacking. According to the financial sector, six savings banks—Yega람, Welcome, DB, OK, Hana, and Korea Investment—have experienced intrusion incidents since late September.

The leak damages are as follows: △Yegaram 43,246 people △Welcome 2,299 cases △DB 142 people △OK 518 people △Hana 552 people △Korea Investment 86,433 people.

The scale of the data breach at Korea Investment Savings Bank is among the largest in the entire financial sector. The only financial institution with a higher number of leaked cases than Korea Investment Savings Bank is the fintech firm 'Moin' (86,504 people), which provides overseas remittance services.

Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

"While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said.

It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts.

As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including -

Names
Email addresses
Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times
Public keys
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters
Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery
Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers

1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

"The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security."

"Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."

Education technology platform Turnitin has disclosed a cyberattack involving certain customer-facing systems.

A subsidiary of Advance Publications, Turnitin provides plagiarism checking solutions used by thousands of education and research institutions worldwide.

“We are writing to let you know that we recently identified unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing Turnitin systems,” CEO Chris Caren revealed in a November 23 letter on the company’s website.

The company immediately initiated its incident response plan, notified the relevant authorities, and launched an investigation with support from external cyber experts.

“We can confirm our systems are fully operational and safe to use and that these customer-facing systems do not collect government identification credentials or institutional financial information,” Caren said.

The company continues to monitor the affected customer-facing systems while its investigation into the nature and scope of the incident continues.

Customer-facing Turnitin systems include the submission portal for students, a grading interface for instructors, integration APIs for institutions, and reporting dashboards. The company did not say if any or which of these systems was breached.

Caren did not say if any data was accessed or how many customers might have been affected, but the University of Colorado Boulder said on Tuesday it was in touch with the company to understand if any CU Boulder information was compromised.

“At this time, we have no indication that student or instructor information, assignments, or other CU Boulder data was exposed. Since Turnitin is primarily accessed via a Canvas integration, OIT has added additional monitoring to ensure Canvas has not been impacted,” the university’s Office of Information Technology said.

Bots exploited leaked AWS key from Docker image in under 8 seconds

A cloud access key left inside a newly published Docker image can be found and used by bots in less than eight seconds, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis of Stony Brook University discovered after planting 300 decoy images on public container registries.

Docker images are packaged copies of software, bundled with everything needed to run it, and developers publish them to public registries such as Docker Hub, which hosts over 14 million of them, so others can download and use them.
Passwords and API keys left in these images have been studied before, and an earlier analysis of over 300,000 images, cited in the paper, found some type of secret in 8.5% of them. Tsouvalas and Nikiforakis wanted to know who goes looking for those secrets and what they do with them.
Over four months, they published 300 copies of the official nginx image on eight registries, including Docker Hub, Amazon ECR and Red Hat Quay. Each copy held decoy AWS, OpenAI and Anthropic API keys.
The images were not advertised anywhere, but the AWS keys still received over 140,000 API calls from more than 5,000 IP addresses, and the OpenAI and Claude keys were drained of their entire balances. The researchers call the scanners behind this activity “ContainerBots.”
“In effect, publication and compromise are, for practical purposes, the same event,” they wrote.
Keys used within minutes
In the first round, all 100 images went to Docker Hub. More than half of the AWS keys were used within a minute of publication, 93% within five minutes and all of them within 15 minutes. The median time to a first call was 51 seconds, and the fastest call came 7.86 seconds after the image was pushed.
Docker Hub’s pull counter lags behind actual downloads by about 5 to 6 minutes. “This means that even a vigilant image owner monitoring their own pull count cannot react before a leaked credential has already been used,” the authors noted.
Bots skip running the images
Each image also had hidden callbacks that would alert the team if someone built a container from it, ran it or opened a shell inside it. None fired in the first round, and only three fired in the second round of 200 images.
The researchers used their observations to reconstruct the likely workflow. A bot queries a Docker Hub catalog endpoint that lists recently published or updated images and fetches each image’s manifest.
The manifest includes the build history, so the bot can tell which layers, the stacked pieces an image is built from, probably hold credentials. It downloads just those layers, unpacks them and searches the files for strings that look like keys or login details, and the whole thing takes a few seconds.
Keys tested first
Almost every bot started by asking AWS a simple “who am I” question to see whether a key worked, and about half of the IP addresses stopped there.
The OpenAI and Claude keys followed what the researchers call a validate-wait-exploit pattern. OpenAI keys saw small bursts of use after each image push, then went quiet for several weeks.
About a month after the last push, a single key received 143 requests in under 24 hours, burning through over 18 million input tokens and emptying the account. The Claude keys were drained in a single day after the image update on day 8.
“We speculate that the wait phase reflects validated keys being resold and held idle until a buyer eventually uses them,” the paper reads.
In the second round, some OpenAI and Anthropic keys had locked-down permissions, and none of them were used to consume tokens. “Not a single Restricted key received any token-consuming call, indicating that scanners are able to discriminate between Open and Restricted permissions,” the researchers wrote.
